ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The soil is one of the most important components of Earth and provides the greatest nutrient reservoir to support the diverse groups of microbes due to its heterogeneous nature. Often, pedigree shifts of microbial communities are seen in soil samples due to the influence of biotic and abiotic factors. Apart from the soil, organic matter is the main driver of acquiring new traits as well as physiological adaptability in microbes. Therefore, it encourages us to make a clear understanding of microbes and their functions from diverse habitats of soil. As is well known, the inhabiting microbes play a crucial role in biogeochemical cycles, plant growth promotion (PGP), bioremediation, and several other interactions. However, we have limited knowledge about the hidden microbial potential that is continuously at work inside the soil system, due to a lack of precise methods for total microbe identification and functional annotation. Omics approaches alone are insufficient to reveal real-time functional information due to several limitations. However, due to the emergence of meta-omics approaches, it is now possible to unlock the complete functioning of soil. In contrast, we can explore multiple facts at a time by minimizing barriers associated with molecular soil microbiology. So far, critical analysis of soil microbes has yielded unique findings, as well as insights into microbial strength, inter- and intra-dependent mechanisms, pathways, and novel biomolecules with industrial applications. This review can provide valuable insights into soil microbial functioning and challenges.

ce:section.ce:para: There is a huge gap between actual knowledge of culture-dependent and independent microbiome investigation, especially in the case of soil samples [1]. Culture-dependent methods are restricted by the growth of total microbes in artificial conditions, and individual independent methods suffer from developing a clear functional profile. To address this problem, meta-omics approaches have evolved. Generally, meta-omics approaches can be covered into four strategies, viz., i) metagenomics, ii) metatranscriptomics, iii) metaproteomics, and iv) metabolomics [2]. Soil exhibits unprecedented opportunity for human welfare; it is an urgent need to exploit the microbial potential present in the soil, but merely traditional-omic approaches are not sufficient to deliver the same [3–5]. Meta-analysis has the potential to bridge the boundaries of studies on soil samples, while linking targeted ecosystem functions [6]. Nevertheless, as meta-omics approaches are introduced, it is not possible to complete the interrogation of a soil sample. The successive turn-up, upgradation, shifting, and transformation of meta-omics are now ongoing to revolutionize various aspects of microbiology studies, especially soil microbiology [4,7]. Here, it is essential to clarify that, despite advancements in molecular tools and techniques such as biomolecule extraction methods (DNA/RNA/proteins/metabolites), molecular cloning methods, and sequencing platforms, it is not possible to accelerate the pace of omics approaches in the soil system, which is required. In addition to the above methods, advancements in statistical tools and bioinformatics are also highly needed [8]. It is utmost importance to discuss the technical sections of soil meta-omics. Integrated meta-omics approaches can minimize the efforts and can gather maximum information about the functional potential of soil microorganisms [9]. Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are a group of consecutive genes present within a variety of microorganisms, such as bacteria and fungi, that can produce specialised metabolites. Goethem et al. [10] identified approximately 3000 biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) encoding secondary metabolites from soil samples through long-read metagenomic DNA sequencing followed by metatranscriptomic validation analysis. The rhizosphere microbial community is as complex as soil and comprises different prokaryotic and eukaryotic species that coordinately perform distinct activities to enhance the growth and development of plants ([11]; Wang et al., [12,13]). The dynamics of plant microbe interaction (PMI) and soil ecosystems have been progressively enhanced through various omics techniques, including metagenomics, metaproteomics, metatranscriptomics, and metabolomics. Therefore, comprehensive analyses of different types of soils with interdisciplinary meta-omics approaches are required to exploit the best of the soil. This article explores various aspects of soil microbiology using a meta-omics approach, which is essential for addressing future challenges.

ce:section.ce:section-title: A brief history of the emergence of soil meta-omics practices
ce:section.ce:para: The history of microbiology is regarded as one of the pioneering areas of study in the field of living organisms. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's early microscopic work on dental plaque in the 17th century showed the existence of microorganisms. Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch were the pioneers in laying down the foundation of soil microbiology in the 19th century. The discovery of nitrogen-fixing (N2) bacteria, Rhizobium from leguminous plants, by Martinus Beijerinck, is a breakthrough in the area of soil microbiology [14]. Sergei Winogradsky further continued the work on Rhizobium and proved its significance in nitrogen fixation and improving soil fertility [15]. Significant progress was made in soil microbiology with the contributions of Winogradsky, Beijerinck, and Selman Waksal. A few literatures also consider Sergei Winogradsky as the father of modern microbiology, due to his pioneering work on nitrogen fixation and sulfur-oxidising bacterium Beggiatoa, which led to the theory of chemolithotrophy [15]. Dutch microbiologist Beijerinck's contributions to soil microbiology are commendable, particularly in his work on nitrogen fixation, symbiosis, bacterial sulfate reduction, and the development of enrichment technology. With utmost advancement in sequencing technology, significant discoveries were documented in the field of soil microbiology, especially in the late 20th century. Massive information was generated through high-throughput sequencing in various domains of microbiology for exploring microbial diversity and identifying their role in improving soil fertility, crop productivity, bioprospecting, bioremediations, and several other areas of biotechnology. Currently, soil microbiology is a much broader field, addressing global challenges such as food security, soil fertility, and climate change.

Next-generation sequencing (NGS) has revolutionised the world of soil microbiology by introducing various omics technologies, viz., metagenomics and metatranscriptomics. This led to the development of metaproteomics and metabolomics, providing deeper insights into soil microbes and their functional attributes. The historical development of metagenomics and metaproteomic studies —a rich tapestry of scientific progress —is deeply rooted in the challenges of culturing soil microbes in the laboratory. Less than 1 % of soil microbes can be cultured using traditional cultivation methods in the laboratory [16]. This is due to the inability to simulate the environmental conditions in the laboratory [17]. Therefore, molecular approaches were adopted to bypass the tedious culture conditions, and community DNA was directly cloned for sequence and function-based analysis of total microbial communities present in an environmental sample. The first metagenomic study documented was based on cloning of 16S rRNA genes of Sargasso Sea metagenomes, followed by Sanger sequencing to explore the microbial diversity ([18]; Fig. 1). A 40 kb insert size came from a marine sample containing a 16S rRNA gene of archaea identified by Stein et al. [19]. Microbiome-based studies were accelerated multi-fold with the evolution of NGS technology. The term ‘Microbiome’ was given by Joshua Lederberg in 1988, which represents the total number of collective microbes present in a sample. Approx. ten years later, the term “metagenome” was coined by Handelsman et al. [17] to uncover different untouched and hidden microorganisms over the culturable microbes in laboratory conditions. Two groups, Handelsman et al. [1] and Burgmann et al. [20], conducted metagenomic investigations independently in the late 20th century. Several enzyme-coding genes, such as amylase, cellulase, xylanase, asparaginases, protease, and pectinase, have been retrieved from soil metagenomes [21–24]. Usually, cultivation methods are unable to recover the Saccharomyces and other yeast species from soil samples. However, the targeted metagenomics approach has unveiled that Saccharomyces mikatae and S. eubayanus have been recovered from soil and bark [25]. Novel polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) degrading bacterial candidates have also been recovered from soil using gene-targeted metagenomics. Additionally, functional facets of soil metagenomics are crucial for understanding the soil microbial ecology at various taxonomic levels [26]. With the advent of sequencing technology, microbial-based ecology gained exponential growth in several facets. However, the analysis of massive sequences generated from the high-throughput sequencers was a big challenge. Fig. 1 includes an expanded interpretive discussion linking the historical timeline of emergence of meta-omics to major technological milestones and their impact on soil microbiology research.

Several tools, such as mother, metagenomics rapid annotation using subsystems technology (MG-RAST), and quantitative insights into microbial ecology (QIIME), evolved to address this issue [27–30]. Schloss et al. [28] developed a comprehensive platform-free software, mothur, to study the pyro-sequencing-based microbial signature sequences. MG-RAST was also developed in 2008, and its first version was released by the Argonne National Laboratory at the University of Chicago for analysing phylogenetic relatedness and functional annotation [27]. QIIME is one of the preferred tools for analysing short sequence reads (SSRs), such as bacterial-specific 16S rRNA and fungal-specific 18S rRNA/ITS signature sequences derived from metagenomic DNA. QIIME1 was the first version released by the Knight laboratory in 2010-11, and it was succeeded by QIIME2 in 2018, which introduced more features and a user-friendly interface. Here, amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were used for taxonomy assignment in place of operational taxonomic units (OTUs). Due to the greater sensitivity of ASVs over OTUs, a deeper resolution (up to a single base level) in species identification was achieved in QIIME2. Massive research has been conducted in soil microbiology using QIIME2 to understand soil microbial ecology [29,31–35]. HUMAnN3, MetaPhlAn, and specialised software are enabling functional association networks and pathway reconstruction. At present, statistical approaches and modeling frameworks are used to analyse high-dimensional meta-omics data, such as multivariate analysis, co-occurrence networks, correlation-based clustering, and Bayesian inference models. This provides readers insights into appropriate methods to infer ecological interactions and functional relationships in heterogeneous soil microbiomes. The explicitly addressing about recent advances in machine learning, deep learning, and artificial intelligence (AI) are applications in meta-omics data interpretation. These approaches help tackle high complexity, identify key biomarkers, predict gene functions, and model multi-layered interactions within soil microbial communities. Muscatt et al. [36] observed that targeted metagenomics are crucial for understanding the soil-bacterial-viral ecology and evolution. The group observed several non-redundant viral OTUs at various soil thicknesses. Siles et al. [37] developed a method to monitor total microbial dynamics, including any changes, by incorporating EL-FAME (ester-linked fatty acid methyl ester), PLFA (phospholipid fatty acid), and qPCR (quantitative PCR) of ribosomal genes.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Why are integrated meta-omics studies needed in the context of soil microbiology?
ce:section.ce:para: To understand microbial community structure and function in an ecosystem, omics strategies are required to gain a deeper understanding of microbial populations. Meta-omics approaches encompass cross-cluster research, enabling the analysis of structure, function, dynamics, interactions, pathways, and in situ and ex situ activities of the millions of microorganisms within an ecosystem. Additionally, community output is assessed using a systems biology approach that identifies the community's interaction network and response towards environmental factors. However, an ecological model will be developed after analysing community structure and function to explain a habitat's combined behaviour and properties.

When multiple approaches are applied to the same sample, they can be linked effectively to the microbial communities with an appropriate function [2,38]. The omics potential boosts the ability of these approaches to uncover the microbial community structure from soil samples and elucidate functional wellness by marking genes and their expression level, novel enzymes and their activity, metabolites and their regulators, inhibitors and control, protein profiles and encoding genes, etc. [23,39]. The potential of these approaches to unlock new information about plant-microbe interactions (PMIs) and self-interactions, active dialogues, microbial network and co-occurrence, nutritional exchange mechanisms, involvement of antisense RNA, bioremediation methods, environmental indicators, and symbiotic relations is truly intriguing and exciting [40]. This excitement is further bolstered by the potential of these approaches to enhance our understanding of soil health and the clear application of recovered biomolecules in sustainable agriculture, bioremediations, chemical, pharmaceutical, food, detergent, textiles, leather, pulp, and paper industries [41]. The explicitly interprets this schematic, explaining key steps of meta-omics workflows and highlighting bottlenecks or innovations at each stage, thereby integrating as a framework to structure the challenges and opportunities discussion in Fig. 2.

The management of big data in microbial diversity research would not have been possible without the crucial role of bioinformatics, which plays a significant role in bridging the gap between microbial diversity and its functional annotation. The continuous upgradation of sequencing platforms and bioinformatics tools, such as analysis pipelines, software, biostatistical methods, and algorithms, is highly necessary to achieve research objectives and deliver trusted informations [38,42]. The introduction of parallel sequencing platforms (2000) and whole genome sequencing (WGS) through shotgun (2004) accelerated the ways of soil microbiology research [43,44]. Advance sequencing platforms such as Roche 454, SOLiD, Illumina, and Nanopore, which are based on sequencing by synthesis (SBS), sequence by ligation (SBL), and electrical signals detection methods, are now widely used in metagenomics investigations [9,45,46]. Detailed information about steps, chemicals, methods, advantages, and disadvantages is discussed in several reviews [40,43]. The microbial community in an ecosystem is linked, resulting in a complex web. Research in this field during the 20th century has been successful in providing insights into a few relationships based on culture-independent approaches. Thus, it enhances our understanding of community structure and functions from diverse habitats. The integrated approach should be able to fill valuable output gaps related to metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, and metabolomics [4,47–49]. Here, we have attempted to provide updated information about methods/protocols used in the meta-analysis of soil samples. Ultimately, we focused on developing a quick understanding of meta-analysis methods and novel ideas for further research. A list of different kits developed for soil DNA, RNA, and protein extraction is given in Table 1.

Metagenomics is a comprehensive area of microbiology that creates a roadmap of microbial community members and identifies functional genes from entire microbial populations present in a sample [1,50]. It gives us unlimited ideas about microbial life's existence and makes value for existence with phylogenetic relations among them [51]. The global scale of several ongoing microbial survey projects, such as the Earth Microbiome Project (EMP), Terra-Genome, the Brazilian Microbiome Project (BMP), the China Soil Microbiome Projects Initiative (CSMPI), EcoFINDERS, and MicroBlitz, demonstrates the collaborative efforts towards the exploration of soil microbial taxonomic and functional diversity [52–54]. This global collaboration encourages the analysis of a comprehensive and significant output regarding soil microbiome potentials. Over the past two decades, the emergence of metagenomic approaches has garnered significant attention in the field of soil microbiology (Fig. 1). This has opened up new avenues for discovering microbiomes and biomolecules from rare soil samples [55]. This approach evolved more rapidly than conventional omics approaches, covering every field of microbiology and garnering increased attention towards soil samples in a remarkably short period. A bibliometric analysis of soil metagenomics studies indicates that between the years 2000 and 2019, a total of 13,543 papers were published, whereas 2212 hits were observed on soil metagenomics only [56]. To date, different aspects of soil are covered, in which sustainable agricultural practices, environmental monitoring, and plant-microbe interaction (PMI) are mainly discussed. Recently, soil samples from two different life zones, tropical rainforests and temperate zones, showed a remarkable diversity of genes nosZ, norB, and nifH, which are involved in the nitrogen cycle [57].

Metatranscriptomics finds huge potential to project a beam of light to express functional magnitudes of the microbial community in an ecosystem [58,59]. Recent advancements in meta-omics approaches, particularly in metatranscriptomics, have significantly enhanced our collective understanding of microbial community structure and their functions in various ecosystems [60]. Furthermore, with the revolution in sequencing technology, it is now possible to perform metatranscriptome sequencing from complex environmental samples and estimate the total number of functional genes present within the microbial community [61]. Additionally, it enhances our understanding of gene expression and network patterns by capturing total RNA molecules from microbial communities. Therefore, it can be used to investigate the pathway of microbes associated with different hosts to confirm their interaction patterns. Henceforth, commonly, unassembled rather than assembled reads are used in soil metatranscriptomics studies [62,63]. Identifying efficient metabolic pathways and enzymes in microbial communities allows us to understand the mechanism of biotransformation and biodegradation of organic chemicals and pesticides in natural conditions [64,65]. It enables the understanding of a map of several pathway types that lead to an understanding of active roles in biogeochemical cycles, phytoremediation, microbes, and host signaling, among others [65,66]. Significant research has been done to understand soil microbiology at the RNA level. In a study, a novel network within all genes was developed [67]. A comparative study was done for soil samples suppressive and non-suppressive to the fungal pathogen Rhizoctonia solani, revealing that stress-related genes (ppGpp) were up-regulated after pathogen infection; it was hypothesised that invading pathogens induced stress response that leads to shifts in microbial community and activated antagonistic traits for defence [62]. Another report suggests that greater expression of polyketide cyclase and terpenoid biosynthesis backbone genes was found in suppressive samples [68]. Baraniya et al. [69] studied the activity of the rhizosphere prokaryotic microbial community before and after sunrise and observed that before-sunrise samples had a higher abundance of phyla Xanthomonadales, Sphingomonadales, and Caulobacterales in comparison to after samples; these changes were identified as due to the response of regulatory genes for both carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism [69]. Henceforth, cataloguing and networking of active genes involved in resistance to heavy metals, bioremediation, plant growth promotion (PGP), and antibiotic resistance may be possible through this strategy [65,70]. In metatranscriptomics, qPCR and microarray technologies have been widely used to analyse soil microbial communities [71,72]. In these studies, microbial identification was performed using Sanger sequencing, but this method has its own limitations. This method revealed relevant information and accelerated soil microbiology research through the quantitative and qualitative identification of rhizomes, antibiotic-resistant bacteria, metagenomes, and viromes [39]. Further, a fungal pathway showed a potential role in xylose degradation activity from Permafrost samples, and a methanogenic pathway that is involved in hydrocarbon degradation from an oilfield sample was also identified [73]. The metatranscriptomics study of tidal marsh communities was done based on hybridisation and cloning of rRNA [74]. At present, Poursalavati et al. [75] reported an updated method of total RNA extraction from soil samples, which is free from contaminations, such as humic acid, DNA, polysaccharides, and effective towards direct sequencing through Nanopore's methods.

It differs from traditional omics approaches due to the advancement in predicting multiple proteins within a limited time frame, rather than the ‘one clone-one protein’ approach. Therefore, it is a targeted approach to announce the total protein in a sample at a given time [76–78]. Several microbes are present in an environmental sample exhibiting several genes that govern their protein profile. Earlier reports on microbial community proteome profiling were found in the human gut and soil. They discuss the technical attributes of metaproteome studies based on total protein extraction, two-dimensional gel electrophoresis (2-DGE), followed by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionisation-time of flight (MALDI-TOF/MS) analysis of certain proteins [79,80]. Extracted protein from soil samples must often improve their high quantity and appropriate analysis methods [81]. The total protein of a natural microbial biofilm was analysed using metaproteomics [82]. For proteome studies, the LC-MS/MS instrument was first introduced to the market in 1989. Furthermore, their extensive use began in 2012 in metaproteomics studies [9,82]. However, nano-liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (nanoLC-MS) techniques are the most powerful technique that identifies 10–1000 peptides and proteins per sample [83]. Since the term metaproteomics was coined, it has led to several breakthroughs in soil metaproteomics research. Numerous studies on different soil samples have been conducted to unveil associated microbial pathways [78,84]. The analysis of the total proteome of soil samples by Wilmes and Bond [78] led to the identification and decoding of several functional genes as well as corresponding mRNA. Recently, a Kaiko de novo pipeline was developed to decode proteomic data into 16S rRNA gene sequencing for taxa analysis [58]. Rodríguez-Ramos et al. [85] identified 10,063,272 proteins from 33 river sediment samples using a Q-Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass analyser. In the absence of metagenomic data sets for a specific sample, the ability to identify the affiliation of a particular query protein/peptide becomes a daunting task [86,87]. Demin et al. [86] reviewed both the above approaches, which are crucial in identifying the ecology, functional, and physiological ways of recycling sulfuryl by sulfate-reducing prokaryotes (SRPs). The identification and correlation of proteins are indeed challenging. However, reports suggest that combined studies will bridge the gap between soil metagenomics and metaproteomics. Nebauer et al. [88] suggested ways to overcome bottlenecks in environmental metaproteomics studies through data analysis steps. Functional profiling of Arctic soils shows the α-/β-/γ-Proteobacteria phyla group is responsible for the acquisition of small and soluble compounds [89]. Both approaches are used for the first time in fungal community and functional strength correlation studies from soil collected across different global biomes [90]. Pan et al. [91] summarised that the combination of metagenomics and metaproteomics can significantly enhance the overall understanding of soil microbial communities, along with their respective functions. So far, these studies are facing difficulties in different interfaces; further investigation of soil samples is needed in the future through advanced strategies.

Soil metabolomics assists in identifying both categories of metabolites, one for which we have a reference database, and the second for the unknown compounds [4]. Swenson et al. [92] were the first to try to link soil crust microbial community structure with their function by using both metagenomics and metabolomics. Metabolomics offers the potential to assess the overall metabolic picture running among the biological soil system, but also has been applied for roles in addressing issues like ecotoxicity due to heavy metals and other pollutants. The complex soil-plant-microbe interactions can also be deciphered through metabolomics. A study by Yang et al. [94] utilised metabolome studies to address complex interactions of Trichoderma longibrachiatum with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in maize. The study suggested that the dual inoculants of T. longibrachiatum with Glomus sp. in this plant can significantly increase salt tolerance activity. Soil metabolomics has been successfully employed to understand the metabolomic profiles, nutrient cycling, microbial dynamics, and responses to environmental changes [93,94]. In a study by Withers et al. [95], untargeted metabolome data were employed to develop a relationship between the soil metabolome and physical and chemical properties of the soil. The work on metabolomic fingerprints has been correlated to formulate soil quality indicators taking into consideration land use, soil moisture availability, pH, and other environmental factors [95]. The vast information network generated from soil metabolomics can guide the planning and execution of sustainable agricultural practices, while also supporting environmental monitoring [48]. Generally, root exudates can significantly influence soil microbial communities, causing the plant-soil feedback (PSF) effect. To date, soil metabolic profiling can provide the utmost understanding of changes in the microbial community due to chemical legacies [96]. However, a better understanding of the soil biological insight process can be achieved by knowing soil-climate feedback (SCF) mechanisms, where the recognition of low molecular weight metabolites is also important [4,93]. Furthermore, this contributes to precision agriculture by providing a deeper understanding of soil functioning, particularly in terms of nutrient availability and microbial activity. Long-term farmyard manure use in agricultural soil can significantly increase the dissolved carbon and nitrogen contents as well as strongly improve the fungi and bacteria correlation networks [97]. It also plays a critical role in developing bioremediation strategies by identifying microbes and metabolites involved in the degradation of pollutants, which is essential for soil restoration initiatives.

Being a heterogeneous medium, soil often has an uneven distribution of microbes. Microbes can flourish in a variety of environments created by soil structure, with some specific sites being perfect for them.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Metagenomics related challenges of soil microbiology
ce:section.ce:para: A wide variety of microorganisms, many of which belong to the "rare biosphere" (low-abundance species), may be found in soil [98]. When that of more prevalent species obscures their DNA, it might be challenging to identify these uncommon microorganisms using metagenomic techniques. Variance in soil properties makes it challenging to provide a true picture of microbial diversity, necessitating meticulous sampling and DNA extraction approaches to ensure that all microbial communities are represented [99]. Notably, those in difficult-to-access locations are represented in metagenomic investigations. Moreover, microbial colonies that are tightly bound to soil aggregates may be marginalised in metagenome studies [100,101]. While examining the microbial population in soil, DNA extraction is a must. This entails breaking open (lysing) the cells of the bacteria that exist in the soil to collect and examine their DNA [102]. Direct lysis of the microbial cells captures a broader diversity of microorganisms in a soil sample [100]. However, the efficacy of direct lysis of soil microbes for DNA extraction is limited due to the adherence of a significant portion of DNA to soil particles, particularly in clay-rich soils [100,102]. Besides, the extracted DNA coprecipitates with humic acid [103,104]. Humic substances (humic acid and fulvic acid) are one of the major impurities in the extracted metagenome from soil samples. DNA and humic acids share similar physical and chemical properties, such as a sugar-phosphate backbone with a negative charge [105]. It chelates the metals required for the optimum activity of restriction enzymes and various DNA polymerases [106]. Therefore, the processing of impure DNA is hindered at various stages (amplification, digestion, ligation, and transformation) of molecular cloning [107,108]. This suggests that the extraction technique is not entirely efficient, as some microbial DNA remains trapped in the soil [102]. Whereas, in the indirect lysis approach of DNA extraction, the microbes are separated from the soil samples through low-speed centrifugation followed by the lysis of bacterial cells from the pellet [109]. Avoiding issues like contamination from humic acids or soil minerals that could impede the procedure is the aim of indirect DNA extraction from soil. However, here, several soil-adhered microbial cells are left in the lysis and thus portray a partial community [100,109]. Microbes that are firmly attached to soil aggregates are another challenge with soil metagenomics [110]. DNA sequencing and analysis are one of the steps in metagenomic processing. Large volumes of data are produced by next-generation sequencing (NGS). Currently, NGS approaches can yield terabytes of raw sequence data from a single soil sample, creating vast datasets that must be handled and analysed using specialised computational power. NGS technologies, such as Illumina, produce short DNA sequences, making the reconstruction of whole microbial genomes difficult, particularly in a complex environment like soil where a wide variety of microbial species are present ([8]; Fig. 2). The genetic potential of soil microbial populations can be understood through metagenomics; however, it does not indicate which genes are being expressed at any given moment [111]. This restricts the use of metagenomic data alone to make direct inferences about microbial activity.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Metatranscriptomics related challenges of soil microbiology
ce:section.ce:para: Metagenomic investigations help us understand the genetic information of the total microbial community in a sample. However, it provides insights into microbial community activity, such as gene regulation at a specific time, the influence of biotic and abiotic factors, etc. (Fig. 2). Nevertheless, metatranscriptomics enables us to understand ex situ gene expression patterns and gene regulation networking in complex microbial communities from diverse ecosystems. The 16S rRNA gene-based reverse transcriptase (RT) analysis detects the presence of active microbial community diversity from diverse habitats [112]. Pure RNA is a prerequisite for RNA-based analysis. Direct extraction and bead beating methods are two established methods for extracting RNA from various environmental samples. Extraction of DNA/RNA from soil samples is another challenge associated with soil microorganisms [113,114]. RNA isolation from soil is more challenging than DNA isolation due to poor cell lysis and the adsorption of RNA in soil. Housekeeping genes are more stable in comparison to other genes, as seen in metatranscriptomics studies. RNA stability is the main challenge associated with the stability of mRNA due to its rapid degradation by RNase [115–117]. The stability of mRNA depends on several factors, such as microbial species, nutritional resources, and abiotic factors. Besides, changes in environmental conditions also trigger a shift in gene transcription rate. The average half-life of E. coli and Bacillus subtilis mRNA is 5min in laboratory conditions. Hence, in most cases, a poor correlation is observed between the protein-to-mRNA ratio for a single bacterium [116,118]. These problems can be overcome by transferring the sample to liquid nitrogen or an RNA preservation solution, e.g., LifeGuard™ Soil Preservation Solution (MO BIO Laboratories, Inc., Carlsbad, CA) immediately after the RNA isolation. He et al. [119] reported that rRNA and tRNA comprise more than 95 % of the total RNA pool from the microbial communities, but mRNA ranges from only 1–5 %. The yield of mRNA obtained from the soil sample is too low for downstream processing. Therefore, additional steps are required to archive enough starting material (total RNA) for further experiments. Several chimaera cDNA molecules are generated during mRNA to cDNA synthesis, and this happens due to multiple template switching during reverse transcription reactions [120,121]. A predictive understanding of gene function in ex situ conditions may differ from actual gene function carried out by soil microbes in situ; this is a special challenge for soil sample studies where direct genetic material extracted from dead and dormant cells, even genetic material trapped in biofilms [61,122–124].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Metaproteomics related challenges of soil microbiology
ce:section.ce:para: Total protein extraction from the soil is also tedious due to the presence of organic and inorganic compounds, and recovery of insufficient quantities of adequate purity. Also, here, co-extraction of humic substance hinders the activity of the protein and interferes with identification, quantification, and separation processes [7,81,89,125–127]. Several approaches have been adopted for analysing the total protein from environmental samples, especially from soil (Table 2). Steps include two-dimensional gel electrophoresis (2-DGE), cut spots obtained in gel and digested with the help of trypsin and analysed by MALDI-TOF/MS technique, which is mainly used for protein analysis [12,13,84,128,129]. The soil metaproteomics methods are facing two significant challenges. The first is the breakdown of total protein extraction by humic acid and related compounds. The second is the generation of data from computational analysis, which plays a crucial role in the research but poses a major issue due to the limitations of available protein libraries [130]. In another approach, heavy metal-contaminated rhizospheric soil protein was analysed, in which the isolated protein was partially hydrolysed and sequenced through liquid chromatography-high resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS) [131]. Obtained sequences from both methods are annotated by comparing the peptide fingerprints with whole genome sequencing (WGS) of organisms or by comparing a part of the protein/peptide with the maximum homology with the protein sequence in the database. It is reported that analysis of proteins directly coming from environmental sources will be a tremendous opportunity to detect biocatalysts that have the potential to degrade pollutants [132]. In a recent report on direct enzyme targeting from environmental samples, in which 2-DGE was performed, and the gel was labelled with fluorogenic lipase substrate para-methyl-umbelliferyl butyrate (pMUB), further high-sensitivity 14 active lipase spots were detected under UV-light conditions [133]. The heterogeneity and complexity of soil samples prevent the origin of signal methods/protocols for protein extraction. It is an emerging approach that facilitates the identification of total proteins and provides valuable information regarding their structure and functions; its outcomes dominate over genomic information [88]. The impact of global variability on total protein extracted from cross-site soil through metaproteomics studies shows that abiotic factors shape the protein abundance of dominant bacterial phyla [134]. A single soil sample is sufficient to summarise a soil ecosystem's microbial functioning [79].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Metabolomics related challenges of soil microbiology
ce:section.ce:para: To gain a better understanding of soil metabolomics, it is fundamentally essential to fill critical gaps, such as untargeted metabolomics datasets, capturing and detecting VOCs, assessing temporal fluxes of metabolites, and accurately mapping ecological correlations with respective functions [93]. Two key analytical methods, gas chromatography-time of flight mass spectrometry (GC-TOFMS) and ultra-high-pressure liquid chromatography-quadrupole time of flight (ToF) mass spectrometry (UHPLC-QTOFMS), are commonly used techniques to detect unknown metabolites through untargeted metabolomics approaches. However, without a reference database, it is difficult to identify and catalogue the unknown metabolites [97]. The identification and characterisation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are crucial for total metabolite studies of soils; however, bias may be introduced at various steps, such as sample processing, detection, and matching with library data references [135]. Thus, multidimensional data interpretation and analysis-based methods have demonstrated their potential in targeting tentative pathways of microbial communities [136]. The featured improvement, incorporating the above aspects, can minimize the rank of technical challenges and develop a clear insight and understanding of the microbial community in relation to biological processes.

Meta-omics approaches are the ultimate way to know the collective microbial potential of soil samples. The applied area is vast, encompassing microbial ecology, particularly in rhizosphere biology, in situ and ex situ activity, bioremediation, biogeochemical cycles and pathways, and novel biomolecules, among others.

The terrestrial life on Earth has been derived from multiple adaptations, and the microbial community of soil habitats has been trait-selected under different local environmental conditions. To date, the evolutionary mechanisms of microbes are not well explored due to a lack of fossil records for most microbial groups [137]. Somehow, the soil microbial ecology, especially that of bacteria and fungi, rapidly evolved due to alterations in factors such as temperature, moisture content, pH, the influx of fresh organic matter, radiation, and terms of agricultural practices, as well as plant succession groups [138]. Philippot et al. [26] critically explained how the soil microbial community is pivotal to synchronising different biological services, not only for carbon and nitrogen biochemical cycles but also in various feedback loops that improve the soil environment, including physics, hydrology, and chemistry. Indeed, it may occur due to their cooperative and competitive behaviours, as well as natural settings such as nutrient requirements, signaling and communication, and active mitigation against biotic and abiotic stresses. However, the microbial diversity of environmental samples has been assessed by analysing conserved markers, such as the 16S rRNA and 18S rRNA genes, using either clone-based or high-throughput sequencing. However, meta-analytic approaches provide a better understanding of the microbial community and its function in different terrestrial ecosystems. In the last two decades, researchers have analysed microbial community structures from different habitats such as bulk soil, grassland soil, oil-contaminated soil, forest soil, rhizosphere soil, biochar, and marine sediments; henceforth, uniform distribution patterns are not found along with changed habitats [139–142]

Additionally, marker gene-based analysis of microbial communities can be used to predict soil physico-chemical variables [143]. Therefore, a storm of information has been generated for understanding the microbial dynamics of various habitats. Winter wheat varieties were cropped in continuous seasons on the same plots with the two nearest sites and found 95 % core bacterial operational taxonomic units (OTUs) are similar, which includes phyla Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Actinobacteria, Acidobacteria, Gemmatimonadetes, Armatimonadetes, Planctomycetes, Candidatus Saccharibacteria, Verrucomicrobia, Firmicutes, Nitrospirae, and Chloroflexi [144]. Microbial ecology monitoring on different ecosystems and human body parts, including brewery wastewater, lake, marine, air, stream, tongue, gut of an infant, gut, and skin, reports that a group of microbes, referred to as conditionally rare taxa (CRT) microbes that exist within 1.5–28 % of the total microbial community [98]. Cross-biomass diversity and functional traits were examined, and it was observed that polar deserts have lower taxonomic diversity as compared to a hot desert sample [145]. The comparison of soil functional gene composition and opposite extremes of environmental gradients allows us to test hypotheses about microbial community and ecosystem functions [146]. Metagenomics has significantly enriched our understanding of the genetic information present in rhizospheric soil.

Mendes et al. [147] investigated rhizosphere microbes through a metagenomic approach and observed 33,346 bacteria and 3320 fungal OTUs per gram of rhizospheric soil. Studies revealed the abundance of Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Actinobacteria, where gamma-proteobacteria-derived non-ribosomal peptide synthetase was found to play a role in fungal disease suppression. An abundance of Acidobacteria, Bacteroides, and Actinobacteria was identified in the rhizosphere of forest soil as compared to the soil samples and presents a classic example of niche effect [148]. Jiang et al. [149] observed a non-significant correlation between microbial communities of the rhizosphere and leaf chlorosis. In contrast, Wang et al. [150] observed that microbial community composition plays a crucial role in protecting grapevines against salt stress by expressing several salt-tolerant genes. Shotgun metagenomic analysis of Panax ginseng (a medicinal herb) rhizosphere identified several denitrification-associated genes exhibiting a role in declining soil fertility, along with significant information on detrimental fungal pathogens associated with the ginseng plant [151]. At present, most of the research for improving crop production using microorganisms either relies on a single bacterium or a consortium of three to four potential bacteria [152]. Considerable research has been conducted on rhizosphere microbiota transplantation (RMT) to enhance soil productivity and protect plants from various diseases and stress [149,153]. Microorganisms can be used as an alternative to harmful chemicals (pesticides and fertilisers) using RMT technology. Most rhizospheric studies focus on plant growth promoting rhizobacteria (PGPRs); however, studies should also aim to analyse the role of other microbes, including fungi, protozoa, and microalgae [154]. The rhizosphere community analysis requires many replicates for each sample to maintain statistical viability, making it difficult to analyse and manage the rhizosphere data [155]. The rapidly increasing technologies, including various software tools, have significantly enhanced the efficiency of studying rhizospheric microbiology, allowing for in-depth research into the structure and functioning of the rhizospheric microbiome. In contrast, metagenomics approaches show significant contributions to representing microbial communities from different habitats, encompassing a wide range of microbes on Earth.

ce:section.ce:section-title: In situ and ex situ activity
ce:section.ce:para: Monitoring the activity of soil microbial communities is a crucial aspect of understanding the functioning of terrestrial ecosystems. The interaction mechanisms between soil microorganisms and their surrounding environments, a field that is still largely unexplored, gain significance in this context [61]. Transcriptional profiling of the total microbial population in a sample provides insights into the potential strength of a complex microbial community. In situ, the activity of a microbial cell is determined by targeting a variety of cell physiological processes. The study of metatranscriptomics, which plays a crucial role in understanding the impact of environmental change on microbial community function, is particularly important. This is because the transcription level controls gene expression that rapidly adapts to changes in environmental conditions [59]. For instance, when two adjacent wheat field soils were subjected to a fungal pathogen, the suppressive sample showed greater expression of a polyketide cyclase, a terpenoid biosynthesis backbone gene, and many cold shock protein (CSP). In comparison, the non-suppressive sample showed a greater expression of antibiotic genes identified as non-heme-chloroperoxidase (CPO) [68]. Recently, multiple nitrogen cycle functional genes have been targeted through chip (NiCE) base technology to assess the diversity of functional genes involved in nitrogen cycling [156]. A comprehensive study of four soil habitats, including rhizosphere, detritus here, rhizome-detritus here, and bulk soil, indicates multiple microbial nitrogen pathways control plant carbon and inorganic nitrogen availability [157]. The decomposition process and biomass construction of the fungal community, utilising decomposed material, can be identified through a combined study using stable isotope probing gene-targeted metagenomics and metatranscriptomics approaches [158,159]. From the mycorrhizal root of Piloderomacroceum, more than 1500 abundantly expressed genes were identified, and their role in protein metabolism, cell signaling, electron transport, terpene synthesis, and other extracellular activities [160]. Wang et al. [12,13] try to link the effect of three crop rotations, including wheat-maize-cotton in different combination steps, to know the soil organic carbon (SOC) content by mining carbohydrate-active enzyme genes.

Metabolomics has emerged as a brilliant approach that offers the advantage of analysing total metabolites in a sample. Wang et al. [12,13] determined the targeted and non-targeted secretion of primary and secondary metabolites present in the rhizospheric microbial community (Wang et al., [12,13]). Metabolomics is accompanied by various strategies, such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), chromatography, and spectrometry, that define the concentration levels of different metabolites secreted within a specific time interval by the rhizosphere microbiome. The metabolic study in higher plants is more complicated as they secrete about 1–2 million metabolites [161]. Despite omics techniques offering great advantages, metabolomics still has several limitations. For example, the rhizosphere comprises thousands of microbes, making it difficult to analyse, manage, and maintain huge amounts of statistical data along with their metabolites. Metaproteomics further strengthens our knowledge of various physiological, ecological, biochemical, and bioremediation processes through the analysis of different structural and secretory components. A study on Rehmannia glutinosa shows proteins produced by rhizospheric microbes are majorly involved in amino acid metabolism and responding against biotic and abiotic stresses [162]. Jouffret et al. [49] suggest that a cascade strategy by combining the metagenome-derived data and available databases at NCBI can significantly maximise the metaproteomic interpretations to understand the functional behaviour of the soil microorganisms.

Metatranscriptomics enables the study of various gene expressions of a microbiome to describe the functional characteristics better. A metatranscriptomic analysis revealed a stronger rhizosphere effect on pea plants when compared to the rhizosphere microbiome of cereals [163]. Another study, performed on cereal grains, maize, and soybeans, suggested that the application of glyphosate to bacterial cells for prolonged periods increases the prevalence of a glyphosate-tolerant bacterium, which in turn affects the metabolism of nutrients [164]. Through metatranscriptomics, the gene expression of multiple genes of the microbiome can be studied when exposed to different kinds of stress. It can also aid in studying the metabolic activities and functions of novel genes. A comparative report on ratoon sugarcane and plant sugarcane suggests greater enzymatic activities, increased gene expression, and catabolic diversity due to more plant microbe interactions (PMIs) in the rhizospheric microbiome. Additionally, it was found that 24.77 % of proteins present in the rhizosphere were added through bacteria that facilitate membrane transport and signal transduction [165]. Metatranscriptomics has wide utility, indeed mRNA extraction and its instability and shorter half-life make it a tedious task; hence, it is necessary to develop robust techniques to extract RNA from rhizospheric soil to efficiently carry out metatranscriptomic analysis.

Excess use of synthetic chemicals like polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polyaromatic compounds, petroleum hydrocarbons, insecticides, and fungicides for increasing crop productivity causes serious damage in agricultural soils [65,86,166]. The soil-associated microbial community plays an active role in the continuous degradation of organic contaminants due to the potential of multifunctional enzymes. However, the plant rhizosphere, the narrow region of soil that is directly influenced by root secretions and associated soil microorganisms, is the most live and dynamic component of agricultural soil, harbouring complex microbial inhabitants with multiple functions. Synergistic interactions between plants and microorganisms are promising methods for removing soil contamination; hence, several studies were conducted to link plant-associated microbes to phytoremediation functions. However, the functional state of soil remediation is currently partially understood; recent meta-omics approaches offering a better understanding. The combination of methods adopted for meta-omics approaches will enable us to understand the integrated activity of plants and microbes, informing microbial ecology management for phytoremediation [167]. A competition-driven model was hypothesised based on rhizosphere plant-microbe interactions (PMIs) and microbial community ecology, as elucidated through metagenomics approaches [168]. Metaproteomics studies for contaminated soils from 2,4-dichlorophenoxy (2,4-D) compound indicate that at least two linked species are actively involved in the biodegradation of chlorobenzene and the role of 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetate dioxygenase enzyme in 2,4-D degradation [132]. Additionally, it is a cost-effective green alternative for soil remediation compared to traditionally used chemical methods, offering other benefits such as biomass for biofuel production, the establishment of pioneer species in the ecosystem, increased biodiversity, and an active role in atmospheric CO2 fixation [167].

The global biogeochemical cycles are undergoing significant changes due to environmental shifts, posing a challenge for future research to unravel their mechanisms. However, the use of meta-omics approaches, with their immense potential for community-based assessment of metabolic and biochemical functions in diverse habitats, is a promising avenue [169]. These approaches, particularly metagenomics, enable us to establish links between microbial communities and their associated functions, especially in the context of complex metabolic pathways [170]. An integrated model could potentially reveal specific functional connections among community members for the exchange of nutrients, energy, defence, and metabolism. Notably, recent research has identified eight dominant pathways in soil nitrogen cycling, although the frequency of nitrogen cycling varies across different soil habitats [171]. Furthermore, phylogenetic analysis has revealed that the Deltaproteobacteria taxa participate in all eight nitrogen pathways. A novel approach has been proposed to estimate the sulfur cycle, based on the minimum ecosystem concept and the relative entropy of protein domains involved in sulfur-metabolism, resulting in a single-value sulfur score (SS) [172]. The rhizosphere soil, enriched with decomposers such as Postia placenta and Catenulispora acidiphila, plays a crucial role in maintaining soil health. Notably, Nitrobacter hamburgensis and Rhodopseudomonas palustris are significantly involved in nitrogen-cycling, while Oligotrophic carboxidovorans is involved in carbon-cycling [173]. Bhattacharyya et al. [174] reported that serine is the principal metabolic pathway for CH4 oxidation in lowland rice fields. Additionally, the carbon and nitrogen biochemical cycles are key processes in rice fields; a study was designed and successfully performed with two different parameters: ambient CO2 and elevated CO2, with varying temperatures. Interestingly, four genera related to methane production, Methanobacterium, Methanosphaera, Methanothermus, and, Methanothermococcus, were absent in ambient CO2 but observed under elevated CO2 condition [174]. In contrast, rhizosphere soils of different crops were successfully analysed through metaproteomics approaches, resulting in the identification of 189 proteins, 72 of which were derived from microbes and involved in various metabolic pathways [175].

Meta-omics approaches have been successfully employed to explore different habitats, such as soil, ocean, and sediments, for the functional identification of novel genes, antibiotics, antibiotic resistance genes, enzymes, and transporters [23]. Several novel biomolecules have been identified from soil samples using these approaches. Few of them are commercialised for large-scale production on an industrial scale. However, the rate of success of functional metagenomics in the case of soil samples is very low, where most of the genes identified from this approach will not be able to express in a surrogate. At present, metagenomics approaches occupy a central position in soil microbiology research; however, the engagement of other meta-omics approaches is truly accelerating the finding related to ecosystem functioning [24].

The history of soil microbe analysis dates back to the 17th century, where the chronology of technical shifts is also recorded according to need. It occurs due to physical, chemical, and biological divergence; therefore, soil is an extremely heterogeneous habitat. Only omics approaches may not enough to provide sufficient coverage of soil microbiome functioning, mostly obtained results shows multilayered biasness. Now, the transmission of omics into meta-omics is well understood; metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, and metabolomics may be used to increase the accuracy of soil molecular biology insights. It can provide full coverage of microbial functioning associated with the diverse habitats of soil by integration of two or more techniques for a sample, indeed the bioinformatics tools are important component to big data analysis. Environmental fluctuations and time-sensitive studies are additional issues associated with soil-based microbial studies. Rapid DNA/RNA degradation is due to nucleases and humic acid demands quick processing of the soil samples. The applied area has evolved rapidly and encompasses most aspects of soil microbiology. Meta-omics approaches assist in addressing microbial community structure and functions across divergent ecosystems and developing a new web of the microbial community to meet the demands of sustainable agriculture and food scarcity. Even the recovery of natural products, including novel genes, enzymes, transporters, and pathways, might serve as an efficient strategy to diagnose and treat worldwide problems associated with agriculture and other soil-related disciplines. It is urgently needed to address the problems of soil meta-omics studies specially focused for impurity removal associated with DNA, RNA, protein and metabolites extraction from soil samples. The integration of mechanical learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) with the meta-omics technique encourages the exploration of the hidden potential of soil.
